properties.name: Montauk Club
properties.description: A Venetian Gothic social club designed by Francis H. Kimball and completed in 1891, ornamented in terra cotta with scenes of the Montauk people. A New York City landmark at 25 Eighth Avenue and Lincoln Place.
properties.photoAlt: The Montauk Club photographed from Eighth Avenue around 1910
properties.photoCredit: Eugene L. Armbruster, c. 1910 · Center for Brooklyn History (public domain)

properties.name: Obama's Brownstone
properties.description: 640 2nd Street, a 1901 brownstone on a Prospect Park block. In late 1984, fresh out of Columbia, Barack Obama shared the top-floor apartment here with his girlfriend Genevieve Cook before moving to Manhattan the following spring.
properties.photoAlt: The full brownstone facade of 640 Second Street in Park Slope, where Obama lived
properties.photoCredit: Real-estate listing photo of 640 Second Street

properties.name: 1960 Plane Crash Site
properties.description: On December 16, 1960, a United Air Lines DC-8 collided in midair with a TWA Super Constellation over Staten Island and came down here at Sterling Place and Seventh Avenue, striking the Pillar of Fire Church. All 128 people aboard the two airliners and 6 on the ground were killed — 134 in all, then the deadliest aviation disaster in history. An 11-year-old passenger, Stephen Baltz, was thrown clear into a snowbank and survived the impact but died the next day. You can still spot the wound today: look up at 126 Sterling Place and the top courses of brick below the rebuilt roofline are lighter and newer where the DC-8's right wing knifed through, and — unlike its two matching neighbors — its ornamental cornice was never replaced.
properties.photoAlt: Wreckage of the United DC-8 in the street at Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place the day after the December 1960 crash
properties.photoCredit: AP file photo, December 17, 1960

properties.name: Old Stone House
properties.description: A reconstruction of the 1699 Vechte-Cortelyou House, a Dutch-Colonial fieldstone farmhouse. During the Battle of Brooklyn in August 1776, Maryland soldiers made repeated, doomed charges against British troops holding the house so Washington's army could retreat — the stand later memorialized as 'the Maryland 400.' The original was buried and forgotten, then rebuilt from its excavated stones in 1934. Today it is a small history museum in Washington Park (J.J. Byrne Playground) at 336 Third Street, between Fourth and Fifth Avenues.
properties.photoAlt: The reconstructed Old Stone House (Vechte-Cortelyou House) in Brooklyn, photographed in 1940
properties.photoCredit: Stanley P. Mixon, 1940 · Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress (public domain)

properties.name: Litchfield Villa
properties.description: Grace Hill, the great Italianate mansion designed by Alexander Jackson Davis and built 1854–1857 for railroad and real-estate developer Edwin C. Litchfield, who developed much of Gowanus and Park Slope. Davis's most celebrated villa, it is a picturesque, asymmetrical composition of a tall round turret and a square belvedere tower in buff stucco, with verandah columns capped not by classical acanthus but by native corn and wheat. The land was taken for Prospect Park in 1868 — the Litchfields stayed on as tenants until 1883 — and the house at 95 Prospect Park West is now the Brooklyn headquarters of the NYC Parks Department and the Prospect Park Alliance.
properties.photoAlt: Litchfield Villa seen through the trees of Prospect Park in a stereoview from the 1870s
properties.photoCredit: Robert N. Dennis collection of stereoscopic views, c. 1870–1890 · New York Public Library (public domain)

properties.name: Soldiers' & Sailors' Arch
properties.description: The Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial Arch at the center of Grand Army Plaza, designed by John H. Duncan and built 1889–1892 as a memorial to the Union Army and Navy of the Civil War. Its bronze sculpture was added by Frederick MacMonnies around 1894–1901: the Army and Navy groups on the inner piers and, crowning the arch, the great quadriga of Victory riding a chariot drawn by horses.
properties.photoAlt: The Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial Arch at Grand Army Plaza, with the bronze quadriga on top, photographed in the early 1900s
properties.photoCredit: Detroit Publishing Co., c. 1905 · Library of Congress (public domain)

properties.name: Brooklyn Public Library
properties.description: The Central Library of the Brooklyn Public Library, facing Grand Army Plaza. Designed by Alfred Morton Githens and Francis Keally and opened in 1941, it is a monumental Art Deco / Moderne landmark whose limestone facade curves open toward the plaza like a book. The 50-foot gilded entrance screen carries golden figures from American literature by Thomas Hudson Jones and C. Paul Jennewein.
properties.photoAlt: The entrance facade of the Brooklyn Public Library at Grand Army Plaza, photographed in 1942 not long after it opened
properties.photoCredit: Gottscho-Schleisner, Inc., 1942 · Library of Congress (public domain)

properties.name: Old First Reformed Church
properties.description: The Reformed Dutch Church of the Town of Breukelen, whose congregation was founded in 1654 by decree of Governor Pieter Stuyvesant. This Late Gothic Revival church at 126 Seventh Avenue and Carroll Street was designed by George L. Morse and dedicated in 1891. Built of Indiana limestone on a granite base with no interior wood or steel, its 212-foot stone spire is the tallest live-stone steeple in Brooklyn and can be seen for miles.
properties.photoAlt: Old First Reformed Church from the corner of Seventh Avenue and Carroll Street, its limestone spire rising over the gabled nave and rose window
properties.photoCredit: Andrey Romanenko, 2012 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: St. Augustine's R.C. Church
properties.description: Known as 'the Cathedral of Park Slope,' St. Augustine's Roman Catholic Church at 116 Sixth Avenue and Sterling Place was designed by the Parfitt Brothers and dedicated in 1892. A High Victorian Gothic pile of rough-faced brownstone with steep slate roofs, it is famous for its unusual German-derived double apse, its great 150-foot corner tower and steeple, and the bronze trumpeting angel perched atop the Sixth Avenue gable. The Brooklyn Daily Eagle called it 'one of the finest examples of Gothic architecture in the country.'
properties.photoAlt: The brownstone front gable and great steepled tower of St. Augustine's Roman Catholic Church seen from Sterling Place
properties.photoCredit: Beyond My Ken, 2013 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: Memorial Presbyterian Church
properties.description: A Late Victorian Gothic Revival church at 186 St. John's Place and Seventh Avenue, designed by Pugin & Walter and opened in 1883. Built of warm Belleville brownstone with a blue-slate roof, it rises from a buttressed corner tower through an open belfry to a broached octagonal spire. Much of its glorious stained glass is by Tiffany Studios. It has been part of the Park Slope Historic District since 1973.
properties.photoAlt: The brownstone corner tower and broached spire of Memorial Presbyterian Church at Seventh Avenue and St. John's Place
properties.photoCredit: Jim Henderson · Wikimedia Commons (CC0 / public domain)

properties.name: Grace United Methodist Church
properties.description: A Victorian Gothic church at 33 Seventh Avenue and St. John's Place, designed by the Parfitt Brothers (architects of nearby St. Augustine's) and built 1882–1883 for a congregation founded in 1866. It stands diagonally across the intersection from Memorial Presbyterian, built of sandstone with terra-cotta trim and Romanesque and Moorish details, its big stained-glass window and gable facing Seventh Avenue and a long buttressed nave running back along St. John's Place. Note the missing steeple: the square corner tower was originally crowned by a tall octagonal cone spire, but it was blown off in the hurricane of September 15, 1944 and never replaced — the tower has stood truncated ever since.
properties.photoAlt: Grace United Methodist Church at Seventh Avenue and St. John's Place, its square corner tower standing truncated where the octagonal spire was lost in the 1944 hurricane
properties.photoCredit: Beyond My Ken, 2013 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: St. Francis Xavier Church
properties.description: A granite-and-limestone Early English Gothic Revival church at 225 Sixth Avenue and Carroll Street, designed by Thomas Houghton and dedicated on May 15, 1904. Houghton trained in the office of Patrick Keely, America's most prolific Catholic church architect, and the parish he served was founded in 1886 by the Rev. David J. Hickey — who named it for his alma mater, Manhattan's Jesuit college. The congregation's first church, a small galvanized-metal "tin church" erected that same year, was moved to President Street when this permanent building replaced it; it still serves as the parish Lyceum. The great corner bell tower, ringed with gargoyles and crowned by a broached octagonal spire, received a 25-note chime in 1932. Today the church shares a parish with St. Augustine's down Sixth Avenue.
properties.photoAlt: The granite corner tower and broached spire of St. Francis Xavier Church rising above Sixth Avenue and Carroll Street
properties.photoCredit: Jim Henderson, 2008 · Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

properties.name: Park Slope Library
properties.description: The Park Slope Branch of the Brooklyn Public Library at 431 Sixth Avenue, between 8th and 9th Streets. Designed by Raymond F. Almirall and opened in 1906, it was the ninth of Brooklyn's Andrew Carnegie–funded branches — originally the 'Prospect Branch,' whose books had begun life in Litchfield Villa. A two-story Classical Revival block of red brick with limestone trim, it has a projecting portico of paired Doric columns under a pediment engraved 'BROOKLYN PUBLIC LIBRARY / ESTABLISHED 1897,' and torches carved into the keystones above its windows and door symbolizing the light of learning. Inside are stained-glass archways, a vaulted stained-glass ceiling, and tiled fireplaces. It was designated a New York City landmark in 1998.
properties.photoAlt: The red-brick Classical Revival front of the Park Slope Branch library on Sixth Avenue, with its limestone Doric portico
properties.photoCredit: Beyond My Ken, 2013 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: Nitehawk Prospect Park
properties.description: Park Slope's movie house at 188 Prospect Park West, facing Bartel-Pritchard Square at the southwest corner of Prospect Park. It opened in August 1928 as the Sanders Theatre — a 1,500-seat brick movie palace decorated in a Moorish style, with a Wurlitzer organ — on the site of the earlier Marathon Theatre (1908). After the Sanders closed in 1978 the building sat empty for nearly two decades, reopened as the multiplex Pavilion Theatre in 1996, and in December 2018 was reborn as Nitehawk Prospect Park, a dine-in cinema that preserved the 1920s balcony, marble stairs, and original plasterwork. (The original Nitehawk is over in Williamsburg.) A movie theater has stood on this corner since 1908.
properties.photoAlt: The Sanders Theatre at Prospect Park West and 14th Street, its marquee advertising 'Hudson's Bay' and 'Play Girl,' photographed around 1941
properties.photoCredit: NYC Municipal Archives · 1940s tax photo (WPA), c. 1941 (public domain)

properties.name: The Long Meadow
properties.description: The great open lawn that is the heart of Prospect Park — about 90 acres of rolling, tree-fringed greensward stretching nearly a mile down the park's western side, one of the largest meadows in any American park. Laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1860s, it was designed as a pastoral counterpoint to the city: a long, unbroken sweep of grass with no buildings to interrupt the view. From the 1880s until 1935 a flock of sheep grazed the meadow to keep the grass trimmed (and to complete the bucolic picture), tended by a shepherd and his dogs; the flock was finally retired to upstate New York during the Depression.
properties.photoAlt: A shepherd and two collies watching a flock of sheep graze on the Long Meadow in Prospect Park around 1900
properties.photoCredit: Detroit Publishing Co., c. 1900 · Library of Congress (public domain)

properties.name: Prospect Park Boathouse
properties.description: The Beaux-Arts boathouse on the Lullwater, built in 1905 to the design of Frank Helmle and Ulrich Huberty, who modeled its white glazed terra-cotta arcade on Jacopo Sansovino's 16th-century Library of St Mark in Venice. Threatened with demolition in 1964, it was saved by public outcry and in 1968 became one of the first buildings in New York City to be designated an individual landmark. Restored in the 1970s and again in the 1990s, it reflects beautifully in the water and today houses the Prospect Park Audubon Center, the first urban Audubon center in the country.
properties.photoAlt: A vintage postcard captioned 'Boat House, Prospect Park, Brooklyn, N.Y.,' showing the arcaded terra-cotta boathouse and a swan boat reflected in the Lake, with people on the terrace, c. 1910
properties.photoCredit: Vintage postcard, 'Boat House, Prospect Park, Brooklyn, N.Y.,' c. 1910 (public domain)

properties.name: Lafayette Memorial
properties.description: A bronze bas-relief set in a broad stele of polished Milford-pink granite at the 9th Street entrance to Prospect Park, the gift of Brooklyn citizen Henry Harteau. Sculpted by Daniel Chester French and framed by Henry Bacon — the same pair who made the seated Lincoln in Washington — it shows the young Marquis de Lafayette in his major-general's uniform, sword-tip to the ground, beside his horse and the African-American groom who braces its bridle (some historians believe the groom is James Armistead Lafayette, the Revolutionary War spy whom Lafayette helped free from slavery). It was unveiled on May 10, 1917 by Marshal Joffre and former premier René Viviani of the French War Commission, then in New York to rally American support after the United States entered the First World War.
properties.photoAlt: Crowds, flags, and a line of policemen at the dedication of the Lafayette Memorial in Prospect Park on May 10, 1917, with French's bronze relief of Lafayette and his horse on the granite stele behind
properties.photoCredit: Bain News Service, May 10, 1917 · George Grantham Bain Collection, Library of Congress (no known restrictions / public domain)

properties.name: Endale Arch
properties.description: One of the first structures built in Prospect Park, a pedestrian underpass beneath the East Drive begun in 1867 and finished in 1868. Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux with assistant architect Edward C. Miller, it was conceived as a portal carrying visitors from the urban bustle of Grand Army Plaza into the pastoral calm of the Long Meadow, with carriages rumbling unseen overhead. Sometimes called 'Enterdale' in early reports, it has a pointed arch, a stepped superstructure rising to a raked coping with a carved flower at its apex, and banded masonry of yellow Berea sandstone from Ohio and reddish New Jersey brownstone — details that echo a Syrio-Egyptian influence. Inside, the brick cross-vaults were lined with white pine and black walnut paneling. After decades of decay it was restored by the Prospect Park Alliance and reopened in 2020, its hidden colors and woodwork — now LED-lit — brought back to life.
properties.photoAlt: A stereoview of Endale Arch from the Long Meadow side around the 1870s–1880s, showing its pointed banded-stone archway, a park bench, and visitors at the tunnel mouth
properties.photoCredit: 'American Views: Brooklyn, N.Y.' stereograph, c. 1870–1890 · Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (no known restrictions on publication)

properties.name: Brooklyn Museum
properties.description: New York City's second-largest art museum, at 200 Eastern Parkway on the northeast edge of Prospect Park. The monumental Beaux-Arts building was designed by McKim, Mead & White, who won an 1893 competition for a vast scheme — had it been finished it would have been the largest art museum in the world; only about a sixth was built, in stages from 1895 to 1915. Its limestone front rose to a grand central portico of Ionic columns reached by a monumental staircase, with allegorical pediment sculpture and a row of figures by Daniel Chester French along the cornice. In 1934, under a Robert Moses modernization, the great front steps were removed and the ground-floor entrance reworked; a curved glass entry pavilion was added in 2004. Its collection spans some 1.5 million works, from one of the finest Egyptian holdings in the Americas to Judy Chicago's 'The Dinner Party.'
properties.photoAlt: The Beaux-Arts Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences (Brooklyn Museum) seen from Eastern Parkway, its columned portico reached by the grand monumental staircase that was removed in the 1930s, the attic ringed with statues and the central dome behind
properties.photoCredit: Detroit Publishing Co., c. 1905–1915 · Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, Detroit Publishing Company Collection (public domain)

properties.name: Congregation Beth Elohim
properties.description: A Reform Jewish congregation founded in 1861, known as the "Garfield Temple" or "Eighth Avenue Temple" at 274 Garfield Place and Eighth Avenue. Its sanctuary, designed by Simon Eisendrath and B. Horowitz and completed in 1910, is a Classical Revival landmark in Indiana limestone crowned by one of the great copper domes on the Brooklyn skyline — a monumental portico of Corinthian columns carrying a pediment and entablature, with a windowed drum beneath the hemisphere. Across Garfield Place, the congregation's 1929 Temple House (Romanesque Revival and Art Deco) served as a cultural center for the neighborhood. Both buildings are New York City landmarks within the Park Slope Historic District. In March 2021, Beth Elohim merged with Union Temple of Brooklyn.
properties.photoAlt: Congregation Beth Elohim on Garfield Place in Park Slope, its Classical Revival limestone facade and great copper dome seen from the street
properties.photoCredit: David Shankbone, August 2008 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

properties.name: Park Slope Jewish Center
properties.description: An egalitarian Conservative synagogue at 1320 Eighth Avenue and Fourteenth Street, housed in a 1925 Romanesque Revival and Baroque-style brick building designed by Allen A. Blaustein. It was built for Congregation B'nai Jacob and rose from the 1960 merger of three South Brooklyn congregations — B'nai Jacob-Tifereth Israel, Tifereth Israel, and B'nai Sholaum — into the institution that bears its name today. The broad Eighth Avenue front carries a great rose window, round-arched stained-glass lancets, and a small copper dome over the sanctuary. Listed individually on the National Register of Historic Places in 2002, PSJC has been part of the neighborhood's Jewish revival since the 1970s brownstone renaissance.
properties.photoAlt: The red-brick Romanesque front of the Park Slope Jewish Center at Eighth Avenue and Fourteenth Street, with its rose window and round-arched windows
properties.photoCredit: Beyond My Ken, February 2013 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: Brooklyn Conservatory of Music
properties.description: A music school at 58 Seventh Avenue and Lincoln Place, housed since 1945 in an 1881 Victorian High Gothic mansion designed by S. F. Evelette for oilcloth manufacturer William M. Brasher — a red-brick and brownstone corner pile whose conical turret and gabled wings recall the Park Slope of the 1880s. The house served as the Park Slope Masonic Club from 1924 until the conservatory bought it; the school itself was founded in 1897 by German immigrants as a European-style classical conservatory (after merging with the Queens Conservatory), and today teaches everything from voice and piano to jazz, gospel, Latin jazz, and African drumming.
properties.photoAlt: The Brooklyn Conservatory of Music at the corner of Seventh Avenue and Lincoln Place, its red-brick Victorian mansion crowned by a conical corner turret
properties.photoCredit: Beyond My Ken, 2013 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: Ansonia Clock Factory
properties.description: The Ansonia Clock Company factory at 420 12th Street — a block-square German Romanesque Revival brick complex designed by Samuel Curtiss, Jr. and completed in 1881 after an earlier plant on the same site burned in 1880. The company consolidated here from Ansonia, Connecticut, occupying the entire block between Seventh and Eighth Avenues and Twelfth and Thirteenth Streets; the Brooklyn Eagle called it the largest clock factory in the world. At its peak the firm offered more than 440 clock models and exported to Europe, Asia, and Australia. In 1929, amid the shift to electric timekeeping, Ansonia sold its Brooklyn machinery to the Soviet Union's Amtorg Trading Corporation — American workers helped install it in Moscow — and U.S. manufacturing ended. The building stood empty for decades before conversion in the early 1980s to Ansonia Court, a residential co-op that still wraps a central courtyard.
properties.photoAlt: A Brooklyn Eagle postcard of the Ansonia Clock Company factory, captioned the largest clock factory in the world, showing the block-square brick complex with smoking chimneys
properties.photoCredit: Brooklyn Eagle Postcard collection, c. 1910 · Brooklyn Public Library, Center for Brooklyn History (public domain)

properties.name: William B. Cronyn House
properties.description: A French Second Empire suburban villa at 271 Ninth Street between Fourth and Fifth Avenues, designed by Patrick Charles Keely and built in 1856–57 for William B. Cronyn, a prosperous Wall Street merchant. When it went up, Park Slope was still country retreat — this freestanding mansion predates the brownstone blocks that would soon surround it. Its slate mansard roof carries ornamental iron cresting and a central half-story cupola with clerestory windows. The Cronyns sold in 1862; by 1898 Charles M. Higgins had made the house his India-ink company offices, with the factory directly behind. Designated a New York City landmark in 1978 and listed on the National Register in 1982, it has housed Slope Music since 1981.
properties.photoAlt: The William B. Cronyn House at 271 Ninth Street, its mansard roof crowned by iron cresting and a central cupola, seen from the front lawn
properties.photoCredit: Beyond My Ken, March 2013 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.name: Everything and a Bathtub
properties.description: 410 Third Street, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues — a plain 1920 four-story walk-up whose fame is entirely in the front yard. Neighbors know it as "Everything and a Bathtub": a year-round jumble of figurines, signs, seasonal props, and lawn ornaments that spills from the stoop toward the sidewalk, with a clawfoot tub holding pride of place. Featured on StoopDecor's must-see lists and a regular stop on the Park Slope Halloween parade route, it is the block's always-cluttered front-yard house.
properties.photoAlt: The cluttered front yard of 410 Third Street on a sunny day, with pinwheels, plastic flowers, signs, and lawn ornaments spilling toward the sidewalk
properties.photoCredit: Google Street View · 410 Third Street

properties.name: Brooklyn Botanic Garden
properties.description: Brooklyn's 52-acre botanic garden, founded in 1910 on a reclaimed ash dump beside Prospect Park and laid out by the Olmsted Brothers. Its best-loved corners are the Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden — designed by Takeo Shiota and opened in 1915 as one of the first public Japanese gardens in America, with a red torii rising from the pond and a Shinto shrine on the hill — and the Cherry Esplanade, whose double rows of Kanzan cherries draw crowds each spring for Hanami. The garden also holds the Cranford Rose Garden, a Shakespeare Garden, and the domed Palm House conservatory.
properties.photoAlt: The torii gate and Moon View House reflected in the pond of the Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, c. 1917
properties.photoCredit: From C. Stuart Gager, 'The Brooklyn Botanic Garden,' 1917 · Internet Archive Book Images / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

properties.name: Prospect Park Zoo
properties.description: A 12-acre zoo on the eastern edge of Prospect Park at 450 Flatbush Avenue, operated by the Wildlife Conservation Society. Its roots go back to an informal menagerie that opened in 1890; the zoo Brooklyn knows today was built in 1934–1935 with CWA and WPA funding to designs by Aymar Embury II and opened on July 3, 1935. The limestone buildings carry Art Deco zigzag bands and F. G. R. Roth bas-reliefs drawn from Kipling’s Jungle Book. The sea-lion pool at the Flatbush Avenue entrance — where California sea lions still perform daily training sessions — has been the zoo’s signature greeting since opening day.
properties.photoAlt: A vintage linen postcard captioned 'Prospect Park Zoo, Brooklyn, N. Y.,' showing the zoo grounds and buildings, c. 1930–1945
properties.photoCredit: Tichnor Brothers Postcard Collection, c. 1930–1945 · Boston Public Library, Digital Commonwealth (no known copyright restrictions)
